One Core’s View

Everything here is what one thread on one core can see. No sharing, no coherence, no core-to-core transfer, no threads at all. What is left is the part you need to reason about a loop and about whether vectorising it will do anything: how much fits, how much moves per access, what a miss costs, and when a wider register stops helping.

AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 · Zen 5, one core L1d 48 KB · L2 1 MB · L3 16 MB 64-byte lines AVX-512

01Four numbers, and what each one is for

Read from /sys, not a datasheet. L1 and L2 belong to this core alone. The L3 is shared with three others, but inside a single-threaded loop it is simply the last stop before DRAM, so it appears here for its capacity and nothing else.

The same geometry drawn as blocks — cores, split L1, private L2, the two L3s and main memory — is in Twelve Cores, Two L3s.

The one arithmetic fact everything else rests on

A cache line is 64 bytes: 8 doubles, or 16 floats. A 512-bit vector is also 64 bytes. So on this machine one AVX-512 load is exactly one cache line, and a 256-bit load is exactly half of one. That coincidence is why §05 and §06 come out the way they do.

02How the cache is organised

The table above has a Ways column and a Sets column, and they are not decoration: together with the line size they are the capacity. Taking L1d as the example, because it is the one your inner loop is aiming at.

03Capacity: where the working set stops fitting

One dependent access at a time, in random order, so nothing can be prefetched and what you see is the real cost of reaching each level. The dashed line is the same walk in address order, which is what a well-formed loop gets instead.

04The line: memory moves 64 bytes at a time

Ask for one value and the hardware moves the whole line containing it. So the question for a loop is not how many bytes it needs, but how much of every line it forces the machine to move it actually uses.

Blocking and vectorising are the same project

Vectorising a memory-bound loop changes nothing — you can watch the speedup decay to 1.0 in the right-hand panel. Tiling a loop into L1 is what creates the conditions under which the vector units pay off. The order is access pattern, then blocking, then width; a wider vector cannot help a loop that is waiting for memory.

06Alignment is binary, not gradual

64-byte lines and 64-byte vectors mean there is no such thing as nearly aligned. Either every vector load sits inside one line, or every single one straddles two.

07The power-of-two trap

The last single-core property worth knowing, because it bites exactly when you start tiling. L1 has 64 sets and picks one with address bits 6–11, so a power-of-two row length advances the set index by a multiple of 64 — which is to say not at all.

At n = 1024 a column traversal costs 7.19 ns per element packed and 0.30 ns with one extra element per row: 24× for eight bytes. An entire column competes for one set of 12 ways while the other 63 sets sit empty. The rule is not “avoid powers of two” but how many factors of two the row length contains measured in cache lines; a row that is an odd number of lines reaches every set. Worked through one bit at a time in Why 1024 Is Slow.

It is worth being precise about what the cache has shrunk to, because the grid in section 02 gives the number directly. If every address you touch lands in one set, the only lines available to you are that set’s row — 12 ways — and your effective cache is 12 × 64 = 768 bytes. Not 48 KB. The other 63 rows of the grid are still there, still powered, and completely unreachable by this loop, so you are running in 1/64 of the cache — 1.6% of it. That is the general shape of the thing: a loop confined to one set gets ways × line, which is the capacity divided by the number of sets, and the more sets a cache has the worse the collapse is when you hit this.

Which is why the penalty is as large as it is. A column of a 1024×1024 array of doubles is 8 KB of data sitting on 1024 separate lines — it would fit in L1 four times over if it were spread across the sets. Confined to one set, 12 of those 1024 lines can be resident at a time, so by the time the loop comes back around every one of them has been evicted. The array did not get too big for the cache; the loop got too narrow for it.

08What this means for your loops

If your loop…then…
walks memory with stride 1the prefetcher hides most of the latency — the single biggest factor
has an inner working set under 48 KBit runs at 4 cycles per access; this is the tile to aim for
is already cache-residentvectorising is worth up to 5.3×; widen the registers
streams from DRAMvectorising is worth 1.0×; fix the pattern or the blocking first
reads one field of a struct per iterationit uses 1/8 of every line — consider structure-of-arrays
indexes a power-of-two 2-D array by columnpad the leading dimension before anything else
uses vector loadsalign the base to 64 bytes, or every load crosses a line

How this was measured

Pinned to cpu0 with the core warmed by high-IPC work before every run, because the governor raises the clock in response to instructions retiring rather than to the core being busy — an unwarmed core sits near 3.5 GHz and returns a stable, reproducible, wrong number. Latency comes from a randomised pointer chase, so nothing can be prefetched; the width and alignment figures come from hand-written intrinsics with four accumulators, so the loop measures memory rather than the adder’s latency.

This page is generated from the .csv files by make_1core_page.py — every figure and number above follows the data, so a re-measurement does not need the page edited by hand. Sources and raw results are in this directory; the notebook version is 1_core_cache.ipynb.

For the rest of the machine — coherence, false sharing, what threads cost each other — see Strix Point Cache Map, and The TLB Cliff for address translation.
